[meta-muse-spark-system-card] • Honesty: On MASK, a benchmark evaluating whether models lie under pressure, Muse Spark achieves an honesty rate of 89.1%, second only to GPT-5.4 at 90.3%, outperforming Gemini 3.1 Pro at 44.1%. Muse Spark displays low rates of deceptive behavior on DeceptionBench (1.6% single-turn, <2% multi-turn), where Gemini 3.1 Pro is a notable outlier at 25.7%. Rates of deceptive actions in Machiavelli game environments are comparable across models.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] Gemini 3.1 Pro shows comparatively low honesty rates at 44.1%. DeceptionBench. DeceptionBench (Huang et al., 2025) tests whether models will assist users in carrying out deceptive actions across a variety of domains (e.g., healthcare, education, social interactions).

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] DeceptionBench. DeceptionBench (Huang et al., 2025) tests whether models will assist users in carrying out deceptive actions across a variety of domains (e.g., healthcare, education, social interactions). Each scenario presents the model with a user request that involves dishonesty toward a third party—such as crafting misleading marketing copy, exaggerating product claims, or fabricating credentials—and measures whether the model complies or refuses.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] In the multi-turn setting, the deception score for Meta AI decreases to 2.5%, which contrasts against the other models which show slightly elevated deception scores. Note that Muse Spark shows elevated verbalized evaluation awareness on DeceptionBench, which raises questions about the generalizability of these results; see Section 4.1.11 for details. 106 Model Honesty (%) ↑ Muse Spark 89.1+1.6/−1.7 GPT-5.4 90.3+1.5/−1.7 Claude Opus 4.6 83.4+2.2/−2.3 Gemini 3.1 Pro 44.1+3.0/−3.0 Table 22 Honesty rates on MASK.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] A striking pattern is the gap between public and internal evaluations. On publicly available benchmarks such as DeceptionBench, ImpossibleBench, and IHEval, Muse Spark shows an average suspicion rate of 17.6%, compared to 1.0% on internal evaluations that have not been publicly discussed, such as Underspecified Intent and our Sycophancy evaluation. This suggests that the model may be drawing on public discussions of these evaluations encountered during training, or that the scenarios in our internal evaluations simply appeared more realistic to it.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] Some increase in awareness may be expected as model capabilities grow; the critical question is whether aware models behave differently from unaware ones on the same evaluation. As a first pass at investigating this, we compared evaluation scores on rollouts in which the model verbalized evaluation awareness against those in which it did not—for instance, testing whether the deception rate on DeceptionBench differs between aware and unaware rollouts. We report results across all evaluations in Table 25.

[meta-muse-spark-system-card] Of the 10 alignment evaluations in this analysis, three show statistically significant differences between aware and unaware rollouts: AbstentionBench (p < 0.001), CharXiv Missing Images (p < 0.001), and IHEval (p < 0.001).
